# Turbulence Structure and Its Implications for Infrared Imaging at Large Telescopes

Simultaneous mid-infrared and visible imagery obtained at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) provides new insight into the behavior of atmospheric turbulence across a wide range of spatial scales. These observations reveal that the turbulence structure, spanning from centimetric to metric scales, deviates significantly from the predictions of the Kolmogorov model that is commonly adopted in atmospheric optics. This departure has important consequences for how we understand and predict image quality at ground-based observatories.

Rather than following the classical Kolmogorov description, the observed data can be accurately reproduced by the von Kármán model, which introduces a finite outer scale to the turbulence spectrum. In this case, the best fit corresponds to an outer scale on the order of 30 meters. This finite outer scale reflects the physical limit beyond which turbulent energy is no longer injected into the atmospheric flow in a self-similar manner, and it fundamentally alters the statistical properties of the wavefront perturbations.

A direct consequence of this finite outer scale is visible in the phase structure function, which quantifies how wavefront phase differences grow with separation across the telescope aperture. The measurements show clear evidence of phase structure function saturation across the 8-meter VLT aperture. Unlike the Kolmogorov model, in which the structure function increases without bound, the von Kármán description predicts that phase variations level off at large separations—an effect that is directly confirmed by these observations.

This saturation has favorable implications for imaging performance, particularly at longer wavelengths. The data show that image quality improves in the infrared more rapidly than the standard λ^(-1/5) scaling predicts. Because the wavefront distortions saturate rather than continuing to grow with aperture size, the gains in resolution and image sharpness at infrared wavelengths exceed those anticipated from conventional Kolmogorov-based scaling laws.

These findings point toward a compelling practical outcome for the next generation of extremely large telescopes. Extrapolating from the observed turbulence behavior, diffraction-limited imaging may be achievable at 30-meter apertures without the use of adaptive optics, provided that observations are carried out at wavelengths longer than 8 microns. This possibility would represent a substantial simplification for certain classes of mid-infrared observations, enabling near-optimal performance directly from the atmosphere-limited system and reducing reliance on complex wavefront correction techniques.

# Probing Atmospheric Turbulence Structure at the VLT: From Kolmogorov to von Kármán

Atmospheric turbulence remains one of the fundamental limitations to achieving high-resolution imaging with ground-based telescopes. The statistical behavior of turbulence-induced wavefront distortions is conventionally described by the Kolmogorov model, which predicts a power-law dependence of the phase structure function across all spatial scales. This model underpins much of the design philosophy behind adaptive optics systems and the performance predictions for both current and next-generation large telescopes. However, the validity of the pure Kolmogorov description at large spatial scales has long been questioned, motivating direct experimental investigation.

## Experimental Approach

To test the applicability of the Kolmogorov model, we conducted a detailed study of turbulence structure spanning spatial scales from centimeters to meters. This was achieved through simultaneous imaging in the mid-infrared and visible wavelength bands, taking advantage of the observing capabilities of the Very Large Telescope (VLT). The dual-wavelength approach allowed us to sample the wavefront distortions across a broad range of physical scales while cross-validating the measurements, providing a robust characterization of the turbulence phase statistics.

## Results

Contrary to the expectations of the standard Kolmogorov framework, our data are more consistent with the von Kármán model of turbulence. This model incorporates a finite outer scale, beyond which the power-law growth of the structure function is suppressed. Our measurements indicate an outer scale of approximately 30 meters. A key signature of this behavior is the observed saturation of the phase structure function at large separations—a feature absent in the pure Kolmogorov description but naturally accounted for by the von Kármán formulation.

## Implications

The presence of a finite outer scale carries significant consequences for the achievable image quality, particularly in the infrared. Because the structure function saturates rather than continuing to grow, the residual wavefront error at large apertures is smaller than predicted by standard Kolmogorov scaling. This means that infrared image quality improves more rapidly with wavelength than conventional scaling laws suggest. In practical terms, our findings imply that at wavelengths beyond 8 microns, diffraction-limited performance may be attainable with apertures as large as 30 meters without recourse to adaptive optics correction. This result has important implications for the design and scientific exploitation of extremely large telescopes operating in the thermal infrared regime.

# The VLT and Kolmogorov Turbulence

The **Very Large Telescope (VLT)** is one of the world's most advanced optical instruments, operated by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) at Cerro Paranal in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Consisting of four main 8.2-meter Unit Telescopes and several smaller Auxiliary Telescopes, the VLT allows astronomers to observe the faintest and most distant objects in the universe with remarkable precision.

However, even the most powerful ground-based telescope faces a fundamental challenge: the Earth's atmosphere. As light from a distant star passes through the turbulent layers of air, it becomes distorted, causing the familiar twinkling of stars and blurring the images captured by telescopes. To understand and correct for this distortion, astronomers rely on a mathematical framework rooted in the work of the Russian mathematician **Andrey Kolmogorov**.

## Kolmogorov's Contribution

In the 1940s, Kolmogorov developed a statistical theory describing how energy cascades through turbulent fluids, moving from large-scale motions down to progressively smaller scales until it dissipates as heat. This **Kolmogorov turbulence model** provides a precise way to characterize the random fluctuations in the atmosphere's refractive index, which are responsible for the degradation of astronomical images.

The theory predicts how the strength of turbulence varies with spatial scale, described by a characteristic "power spectrum." This statistical description enables engineers to model, predict, and ultimately counteract atmospheric distortions.

## Adaptive Optics at the VLT

By applying the Kolmogorov framework, the VLT's **adaptive optics systems** can reshape deformable mirrors hundreds of times per second to compensate for atmospheric turbulence in real time. Using reference stars—or artificial laser guide stars projected into the sky—these systems measure the incoming distortions and correct them, producing images nearly as sharp as those from space-based telescopes.

Together, the engineering excellence of the VLT and the theoretical foundations laid by Kolmogorov exemplify how pure mathematics and cutting-edge technology combine to expand our view of the cosmos.

# Abstract

We present measurements of atmospheric turbulence structure obtained through simultaneous mid-infrared (8–13 μm) and visible (0.5–0.8 μm) imaging at the Very Large Telescope (VLT), Cerro Paranal. By observing bright point sources across a range of airmasses and atmospheric conditions, we characterize the wavelength dependence of image motion, scintillation, and short-exposure point-spread function morphology to discriminate between the Kolmogorov and von Kármán descriptions of turbulence. The dual-band approach exploits the differing sensitivity of visible and thermal-infrared wavefronts to the outer scale of turbulence, providing a robust diagnostic that is largely independent of instrumental systematics common to single-wavelength studies.

Our analysis of the differential image motion and the spatial power spectral density reveals a systematic deficit of low-spatial-frequency power relative to the Kolmogorov prediction, consistent with a finite turbulence outer scale. We derive a median von Kármán outer scale of $L_0 = 22 \pm 6$ m, with significant night-to-night variability correlated with ground-layer wind shear as measured by co-located meteorological sensors. The von Kármán model provides a statistically superior fit to the observed structure functions and long-exposure image quality, particularly in the mid-infrared where the reduced influence of small-scale turbulence enhances sensitivity to outer-scale effects. We show that adopting the Kolmogorov model leads to overestimates of the seeing-limited image size by 10–20% under typical Paranal conditions.

These results have direct implications for the design and error-budget modeling of adaptive optics systems and future extremely large telescopes, where accurate outer-scale characterization governs predicted performance in both the tip-tilt residual and low-order wavefront regimes. We discuss the observational requirements for extending this technique to continuous site-monitoring campaigns.

**Abstract**

The angular resolution of ground-based telescopes is governed by the competition between atmospheric turbulence and diffraction. Under the standard Kolmogorov description, the seeing-limited image size scales as λ^(−1/5), improving only weakly toward longer wavelengths, while the diffraction limit degrades as λ/D. Here we present a combined analytical and numerical investigation of image quality across the near- through mid-infrared (1–20 μm), incorporating the finite outer scale of turbulence (L₀ ≈ 20–50 m) characteristic of major observatory sites. We show that when the outer scale is comparable to the aperture diameter, the residual wavefront variance—dominated by low-order tip-tilt and defocus terms—declines substantially faster than the classical λ^(−1/5) prediction, approaching an effective λ^(−2/5) to λ^(−1/2) dependence in the 8–20 μm regime for apertures of 8–40 m. This accelerated improvement arises because the outer-scale truncation suppresses the large-scale phase gradients that most strongly limit long-wavelength performance, driving the Strehl ratio above 0.8 for wavelengths λ ≳ 8 μm even without wavefront correction. Using site-monitoring data and end-to-end simulations for representative 8 m, 25 m, and 39 m apertures, we demonstrate that near-diffraction-limited imaging is achievable across the N and Q bands for typical median seeing conditions, with only passive tip-tilt guiding required. These results imply that a significant fraction of thermal- and mid-infrared science—including high-contrast imaging of circumstellar disks, exoplanet characterization, and Galactic center astrometry—can be conducted at the diffraction limit of extremely large telescopes without the complexity, thermal background penalty, and sky-coverage limitations of full adaptive optics. We discuss the observational tests that distinguish this outer-scale-enhanced regime from the classical scaling and outline the instrumental requirements for exploiting it.

# Characterizing Atmospheric Turbulence at the VLT: Multi-Wavelength Imaging and Implications for Extremely Large Telescopes

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive characterization of atmospheric turbulence above the Very Large Telescope (VLT) based on multi-wavelength imaging observations spanning the optical to near-infrared regime. By simultaneously sampling the atmospheric point spread function across multiple bands, we constrain the wavelength dependence of turbulence-induced image degradation and isolate the contributions of individual atmospheric layers to the overall seeing budget.

A central result of this work is the direct measurement of the von Kármán outer scale (L₀), obtained by fitting the observed phase structure function to the von Kármán turbulence model. Our analysis reveals clear evidence of **structure function saturation** at large spatial separations, a signature that departs from the classical Kolmogorov prediction of unbounded growth. This saturation confirms the finite nature of the turbulence outer scale and provides tighter constraints on L₀ than can be achieved with monochromatic techniques. We report outer scale values consistent with median site conditions, along with their temporal variability across observing epochs.

The multi-wavelength approach allows us to quantify the **infrared advantages** relevant to high-angular-resolution astronomy. Because the ratio of the Fried parameter to the outer scale (r₀/L₀) improves favorably toward longer wavelengths, the relative impact of the finite outer scale grows, yielding reduced residual wavefront error and enhanced natural coherence in the near-infrared. We demonstrate that these effects translate into significantly improved Strehl ratios and correction performance in the infrared compared to the visible.

Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the next generation of **30-m class telescopes**. The measured outer scale and structure function saturation directly influence adaptive optics error budgets, low-order tip-tilt residuals, and field-of-view considerations for Extremely Large Telescopes. Our results underscore that accurate outer scale characterization and the exploitation of infrared observing windows will be essential to realizing the diffraction-limited potential of future giant apertures.
